title: P-block: group trends and first-element exceptions
subject: Chemistry

sources.title: Andrew R. Barron: phosphorus oxides and oxoacids

chapters.title: Map groups from valence electrons
chapters.formula: Groups 13–18: ns²np¹ through ns²np⁶
chapters.script: Welcome to P Block Chemistry. This recorded class uses an AI generated Marin voice. The p block spans groups thirteen to eighteen. In the usual main group pattern, the outer s subshell contains two electrons, while the outer p subshell contains one through six. Three outer electrons correspond to group thirteen, and eight correspond to group eighteen. Helium is the important exception: its filled first shell has only two electrons, yet its chemical behaviour places it with the noble gases. An outer three s two, three p three configuration belongs to period three and group fifteen. The period identifies the outer principal shell, while the group reflects the main group valence pattern. Across a typical period, increasing effective nuclear attraction generally reduces radius and increases nonmetallic character. Down a group, additional occupied shells generally increase size and metallic character. These are starting trends rather than complete predictions of every property. Before comparing melting points, distinguish molecular substances, metallic structures and extended networks; they need not follow the same smooth pattern.
points: ns²np¹ · 3 · 13
ns²np³ · 5 · 15
ns²np⁶; He exception · 8; He has 2 · 18

chapters.title: First-member differences and lower states
chapters.formula: Small second-period atoms; inert-pair trends in heavier members
chapters.script: The first p block members differ from heavier members for structural reasons. Boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine have small second period valence shells. Their size, electronegativity and orbital overlap affect which bonds and structures are favoured. They cannot be treated as if their valence shells expand arbitrarily to imitate every heavier congener. Saying anomalous is only a label; a useful explanation identifies the bonding or electronic cause. Among several heavier groups, a lower oxidation state becomes more important relative to the group maximum. This is commonly discussed through the inert pair effect. Thallium plus one and lead plus two are examples of lower states becoming relatively stable. It does not mean higher oxidation states never occur, or that the outer s electrons are unavailable in every compound. Oxidation state stability depends on the actual ligands, bonding and reaction environment. A group number identifies possible electron bookkeeping patterns, but cannot by itself establish which compound is most stable. Compare specified species rather than treating the trend as an absolute prohibition.

Tl(I) · Lower state important · Tl(III) still exists

chapters.title: Groups 13 and 14: deficiency and networks
chapters.formula: Shared group does not require identical structures
chapters.script: Group thirteen commonly shows oxidation state plus three, while plus one becomes important for some heavier members. Boron is a nonmetal and often forms covalent, electron deficient structures. Aluminium has stronger metallic character. Boron trifluoride is a useful Lewis acid example: it can accept an electron pair from a suitable donor. Do not rank all Lewis acids from one octet drawing alone, because bonding interactions and the reacting partner matter. Group fourteen includes carbon and silicon together with more metallic heavier elements. Carbon forms strong carbon carbon bonds, supporting extensive catenation and many stable multiple bonds. Silicon's larger orbitals and different overlap lead to different structures. Carbon dioxide consists of discrete molecules, while common solid silicon dioxide is an extended network of silicon oxygen bonds. A formula ratio of one central atom to two oxygens therefore does not imply identical physical properties. Plus four and plus two states also change in relative importance down group fourteen. Use the group pattern to organize a comparison, then inspect the actual bonding and structure.
points: BF₃ · Electron-pair acceptor · Lewis acid
CO₂ · Discrete molecules · Molecular substance

chapters.title: Group 15: nitrogen and heavier hydrides
chapters.formula: Outer shell: ns²np³
chapters.script: Group fifteen has two outer s electrons and three outer p electrons. Common oxidation states include minus three, plus three and plus five, depending on the atoms bonded to the element. Nitrogen's strong nitrogen nitrogen triple bond helps explain the relatively low reactivity of molecular nitrogen under ordinary conditions. That statement concerns the molecule, not a claim that every nitrogen compound is unreactive. Nitrogen also cannot simply imitate every five coordinate structure of a heavier group member. For the common hydride comparison, ammonia is more basic than the heavier hydrides in the usual introductory sequence. Thermal stability also generally decreases down that series. Ammonia's intermolecular hydrogen bonding makes its boiling behaviour unusual compared with a simple increase based only on molar mass. Basicity, thermal stability and boiling point are different properties: one ordering must not be copied automatically into another column. State which compounds are being compared and what conditions apply. A lone pair may be present in several hydrides while its availability and the stability of the protonated product still differ.
points: N₂ reactivity · Strong N≡N bond · Molecule-specific

chapters.title: Group 16: oxygen and hydride trends
chapters.formula: Oxidation number needs the actual formula
chapters.script: Group sixteen has six outer electrons in the usual main group pattern. Oxygen commonly has oxidation number minus two, but that value is not universal. Peroxides, superoxides and oxygen fluorine compounds require different assignments. Sulfur and heavier members can also have positive oxidation states in suitable compounds. Write the actual formula and apply charge balance instead of turning group membership into a fixed ionic charge. Water has unusually strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding compared with nearby heavier group sixteen hydrides. Its boiling point therefore departs from a simple mass based comparison. In the elementary hydride series, acidity generally increases toward heavier members as the element hydrogen bond becomes easier to break, while thermal stability decreases. Acidity concerns proton transfer under specified conditions; boiling concerns separation of molecules into vapour. These processes should not be treated as one trend. In a ranking problem, identify the property before applying an arrow down the periodic table. Later worked examples will use peroxide, superoxide and oxygen difluoride to check oxygen bookkeeping directly.
points: O oxidation number · Often −2 · Important exceptions
Water boiling point · Raised by H bonding · Intermolecular property
Heavier hydrides · Acidity rises; stability falls · Specified series and conditions

chapters.title: Halogens: three different attraction measures
chapters.formula: Electronegativity ≠ electron gain ≠ aqueous oxidizing strength
chapters.script: Group seventeen has seven outer electrons and commonly forms compounds in which the halogen has oxidation number minus one. Fluorine is assigned minus one in its compounds, while heavier halogens can have positive oxidation states when bonded to more electronegative partners. Near room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. Increasing polarizability strengthens dispersion attractions down the molecular series. Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, yet chlorine has a more negative first electron gain enthalpy. An incoming electron encounters stronger repulsion in fluorine's compact shell, producing this familiar exception. Aqueous oxidizing strength involves several energy changes, so electron gain enthalpy alone cannot determine the complete ranking. Fluorine remains a very strong oxidizing agent in ordinary aqueous comparisons. Hydrogen fluoride is a weak acid in dilute water compared with the usual strong hydrogen chloride, bromide and iodide acids. Its strong bond and the solution environment matter. Keep these different properties and their definitions in separate columns when explaining halogen trends.
points: Electronegativity · F greater than Cl · Bond electron attraction
First electron gain · Cl more negative than F · Compact-shell repulsion
Physical state · Cl₂ gas; Br₂ liquid; I₂ solid · Growing dispersion forces

chapters.title: Noble gases and the meaning of inert
chapters.formula: Filled shells reduce ordinary reactivity
chapters.script: Noble gases have filled valence shells, making many ordinary reactions unfavourable. Their atoms are normally monatomic rather than joined into the familiar diatomic molecules of halogens. Weak dispersion attractions help explain their low boiling temperatures. Down the group, increasing polarizability generally raises boiling points, while the outer electrons become easier to remove. A filled shell therefore does not give identical physical properties to every member. Heavier noble gases can form compounds under suitable conditions. Xenon compounds with strongly electronegative partners show why inert is a contextual description rather than a rule forbidding all bonding. Helium's very small filled first shell is particularly resistant to ordinary chemical bonding and is a distinctive first member. Do not infer that a helium configuration requires six p electrons: helium has a filled first s subshell. When comparing reactivity, identify the species and conditions instead of assigning every group eighteen atom an absolute inability to react. Physical trends and exceptional chemical compounds provide complementary evidence about the same group.
points: Filled valence shell · Low ordinary reactivity · Not absolute impossibility

chapters.title: Read data before applying a trend
chapters.formula: Property → species → direction → exceptions
chapters.script: A reliable comparison starts by naming the property. Radius, ionization energy, acidity, boiling point and oxidation state stability describe different processes. Next identify whether the objects are elements, ions or compounds, and whether the change is across a period or down a group. Only then apply the relevant broad trend. Carbon dioxide compared with silicon dioxide is mainly a bonding and structure comparison. Ammonia and water highlight intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Chlorine compared with fluorine highlights the difference between electron gain and electronegativity. These examples do not justify applying one exception to every unrelated property. If a numerical table is supplied, read its units, temperature, pressure and radius or energy convention. The data are evidence to interpret, rather than an inconvenience to replace with a memorized slogan. In a written explanation, connect the observation with shell size, shielding, orbital overlap or intermolecular attraction as appropriate. Finally check the first member and any unusual structure before deciding whether the broad ordering is suitable.
points: CO₂ versus SiO₂ · Structure and physical form · Molecule versus network
NH₃ or H₂O anomaly · Boiling point · Hydrogen bonding
Cl versus F · First electron gain · Crowding and convention

chapters.title: Worked oxidation numbers for oxygen
chapters.formula: H₂O₂: −1; KO₂: average −½; OF₂: +2
chapters.script: Oxidation numbers are formal bookkeeping values that must add to the species charge. In hydrogen peroxide, take hydrogen as plus one. Two hydrogen atoms contribute plus two, so the two oxygens together contribute minus two. Each oxygen is assigned minus one. In potassium superoxide, potassium contributes plus one and the oxygen pair together contributes minus one. The average oxidation number per oxygen is therefore minus one half. A fractional average is not a statement that an individual atom contains half an electron; it describes the bookkeeping of the bonded species. In oxygen difluoride, each fluorine is minus one. The oxygen must be plus two so the neutral molecule's total is zero. Compare these with water, where oxygen is minus two. The same element can have several assignments because its bonded partners and connectivity differ. Apply the sum rule to the actual formula first. A memorized oxygen value is useful as a common case, but it must yield to a stated peroxide, superoxide or fluorine containing exception.
points: KO₂ · (+1) + 2x = 0 · Average −½

chapters.title: Compare hydrides without mixing properties
chapters.formula: Boiling, acid strength and stability are separate questions
chapters.script: Hydrogen bonding can strongly affect boiling without giving the same ordering for acidity. Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride are familiar hydrogen bonding examples from different groups. Compare each with an appropriate set of related hydrides rather than mixing all group members into one unexplained ranking. Down the heavier hydrogen halides, decreasing hydrogen halogen bond strength supports stronger acidity in the usual dilute aqueous comparison. Hydrogen fluoride remains the weak member of that elementary acid series despite fluorine's high electronegativity. For group sixteen hydrides, acidity generally increases as the central atom becomes larger and its covalent bond to hydrogen weakens, while water has a high boiling point because of attractions between molecules. In group fifteen, ammonia's basicity and hydrogen bonding again require separate explanations. A question about thermal stability asks how readily a compound decomposes under stated conditions, not how much energy is needed simply to boil it. Use the property definition, relevant bond or intermolecular interaction and stated medium to build the comparison. The practice questions combine these distinctions with oxidation number calculations.
points: Boiling point · Separate molecules · Ignore H bonding
Acid strength · Proton transfer in medium · Use electronegativity alone
Thermal stability · Chemical decomposition · Confuse with boiling

chapters.title: Compare nitrogen and molecular white phosphorus
chapters.formula: N₂: one triple bond; P₄: six P–P single bonds
chapters.script: The molecular forms of nitrogen and white phosphorus illustrate why the first member of a p block group cannot simply be copied onto its heavier congeners. Ordinary molecular nitrogen has two atoms joined by a strong triple bond, represented by one sigma and two pi components. Molecular white phosphorus instead contains four phosphorus atoms at the vertices of a tetrahedron. Each phosphorus is connected to the other three through single bonds. Counting four vertices times three connections and dividing by two gives six phosphorus phosphorus bonds, because each edge was counted from both ends. Twenty valence electrons are available in one molecule containing four phosphorus atoms. Six ordinary two electron bonds use twelve, leaving eight electrons as four lone pairs, one on each atom in the elementary Lewis description. The tetrahedral drawing describes this molecular allotrope, not every solid form of phosphorus. Red and black phosphorus have different extended structures. Likewise, a larger total bond count in one molecule does not by itself prove greater chemical stability than another substance; bond strengths, geometry and reaction products matter. Use these structures as examples of catenation and multiple bonding trends, with the molecular identity and allotrope stated explicitly.
points: N₂ molecule · One σ plus two π components · Strong triple bond
Molecular white P₄ · 4 vertices × 3 neighbours / 2 · 6 P–P single bonds
P₄ valence electrons · 20 − 12 in bonds · 4 lone pairs

chapters.title: Account for electron-deficient diborane
chapters.formula: B₂H₆: 12 valence electrons; four terminal bonds and two 3-centre bridges
chapters.script: Diborane provides a supporting example of electron deficient bonding in boron chemistry. Two boron atoms contribute six valence electrons and six hydrogen atoms contribute six more, making twelve in total. Four terminal boron hydrogen bonds use eight electrons in the ordinary two centre two electron description. Four electrons remain for two bridging boron hydrogen boron units. Each bridge is described by a three centre two electron bond, so its electron pair is shared across three atoms rather than assigned independently to both drawn boron hydrogen arms. Two bridge arms therefore do not represent two separate ordinary electron pairs. The molecule contains four terminal hydrogens and two bridging hydrogens. This bookkeeping explains why a conventional drawing with an ordinary two electron bond on every apparent connection would overcount the available electrons. A connectivity projection is useful, but it should not be mistaken for a complete three dimensional orbital picture. The example illustrates boron's tendency toward electron deficient structures; it does not turn every boron compound into the same bonding pattern. This class uses the compound to explain a group trend, not to prescribe its preparation or imply that every historical borane reaction is required by the current syllabus.
points: Available valence electrons · 2×3 + 6×1 · 12 electrons
Four terminal B–H bonds · 4 × 2 electrons · 8 electrons
Two B–H–B bridges · 2 × 2 electrons · 4 electrons; 2 bridging H

chapters.title: Hydrolysis is a chemical comparison not a formula trick
chapters.formula: SiCl₄ + 4H₂O → Si(OH)₄ + 4HCl: schematic initial accounting
chapters.script: Carbon tetrachloride and silicon tetrachloride share a one to four formula ratio and tetrahedral molecular geometry, but that does not give them identical reactions with water. Carbon tetrachloride resists hydrolysis under ordinary comparison conditions, whereas silicon tetrachloride reacts readily. A useful initial accounting representation for silicon replaces four chlorine atoms by four hydroxyl groups, giving silicon with four hydroxyl groups and four hydrogen chloride units from four waters. Subsequent condensation can give hydrated silica; an idealized overall equation ending at silicon dioxide uses two waters per silicon tetrachloride and gives four hydrogen chlorides. The actual condensed product and hydration depend on conditions. The contrast reflects differences in the central atoms, bond interactions and accessible reaction pathways. It should not be reduced to the claim that an empty d orbital alone explains every hydrolysis reaction. Nor should either observation be generalized to all carbon or silicon halides without checking the compound. These equations are atom bookkeeping for a supplied chemical comparison, not a mixing procedure. Distinguish the initial substitution accounting from a net equation that also incorporates condensation and water loss.
points: CCl₄ versus SiCl₄ · Same tetrahedral formula pattern · Different hydrolysis behaviour
Initial Si accounting · SiCl₄ + 4H₂O · Si(OH)₄ + 4HCl
Idealized condensed endpoint · SiCl₄ + 2H₂O · SiO₂ + 4HCl

chapters.title: Separate two useful oxoacid comparisons
chapters.formula: Same central atom: additional oxygen commonly strengthens the oxoacid trend
chapters.script: Oxoacid comparisons need a stated structural family. For chlorine oxoacids, the usual increasing acid strength trend runs from hypochlorous acid through chlorous and chloric acids to perchloric acid. Their formulas contain one, two, three and four oxygen atoms respectively. Assigning hydrogen plus one and oxygen minus two gives chlorine oxidation states plus one, plus three, plus five and plus seven. Additional oxygen helps stabilize the conjugate base through the electronic effects and delocalization appropriate to each structure. This is different from comparing hypohalous acids that each contain one oxygen: hypochlorous acid is stronger than the corresponding bromine acid, which is stronger than the iodine acid in the usual comparison. Here the central atom changes while the oxygen count is held fixed. Do not combine the two patterns into a rule that ignores molecular structure. Strong acids can also be levelled by water, so complete ionization or a single p H measurement at equal nominal concentration is not a universal way to distinguish their intrinsic strengths. The useful method is to identify the acid family, write a plausible conjugate base and then apply the appropriate controlled comparison.
points: HClO; HClO₂; HClO₃; HClO₄ · Cl oxidation states · +1; +3; +5; +7
Same central chlorine · More oxygen in this family · Usual acid strength increases
HOCl; HOBr; HOI · Same oxygen count · HOCl > HOBr > HOI

chapters.title: Read interhalogen formulas and molecular shapes
chapters.formula: ClF₃: AX₃E₂, T-shaped; BrF₅: AX₅E, square pyramidal
chapters.script: Interhalogen formulas combine different halogen elements and provide useful oxidation state and shape examples. In chlorine trifluoride, assign each fluorine minus one, making chlorine plus three. The molecule has twenty eight valence electrons. Three chlorine fluorine bonds use six and the terminal fluorine lone pairs use eighteen, leaving four electrons as two central lone pairs. Five electron domains give a trigonal bipyramidal domain arrangement and a T shaped atomic geometry in the elementary valence shell model. In bromine pentafluoride, bromine is plus five and the molecule has forty two valence electrons. Five bonds use ten and the terminal fluorine lone pairs thirty, leaving one central lone pair. Six domains give an octahedral domain arrangement with square pyramidal molecular shape. The shape names refer to atomic positions, not to a count of electron pairs drawn as atoms. These examples do not assign positive oxidation states to fluorine or prove that every halogen forms every possible formula. Electron counting and domain geometry organize the comparison without requiring a literal claim that a simple hybrid label completely describes hypervalent bonding in the real molecule.
points: ClF₃: 28 valence electrons · 6 bonding + 18 terminal + 4 central · AX₃E₂; T-shaped
BrF₅: 42 valence electrons · 10 bonding + 30 terminal + 2 central · AX₅E; square pyramidal

chapters.title: Boric acid accepts a pair rather than losing three protons
chapters.formula: B(OH)₃ + 2H₂O ⇌ B(OH)₄⁻ + H₃O⁺
chapters.script: The three hydrogens in boric acid do not make it a tribasic acid in its usual aqueous behaviour. Boric acid acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair from hydroxide to form tetrahydroxyborate. One useful net equation writes boric acid plus two waters in equilibrium with tetrahydroxyborate and hydronium. Check the inventory: both sides contain one boron, five oxygens and seven hydrogens, with total charge zero. In the elementary structural description, the boron environment changes from three coordinate in boric acid to four coordinate in the borate product. The familiar description as a weak monobasic acid refers to this aqueous acid base behaviour, not removal of all three written hydrogens as independent protons. Its formal formula alone is insufficient for predicting acid basicity. The equation describes an equilibrium, so it does not mean every boric acid molecule converts completely in water. Other ligands and solution conditions can change speciation. Use electron pair acceptance, the actual product and charge balance together.

chapters.title: Phosphorus oxoacid basicity follows O–H connectivity
chapters.formula: H₃PO₂: 1 OH; H₃PO₃: 2 OH; H₃PO₄: 3 OH
chapters.script: Phosphorus oxoacids illustrate why a molecular formula does not reveal every acidic hydrogen. In the usual structural descriptions, hypophosphorous acid has one oxygen hydrogen group and two phosphorus hydrogen bonds. Phosphorous acid has two oxygen hydrogen groups and one phosphorus hydrogen bond. Phosphoric acid has three oxygen hydrogen groups and no phosphorus hydrogen bond. Their ordinary aqueous acid basicities are therefore one, two and three respectively. The phosphorus hydrogen bonds are not counted as ordinary ionizable protons in this comparison. All three formulas contain three hydrogens, yet their neutralization capacities differ. In a stipulated complete neutralization model, zero point zero one zero zero mole phosphorous acid consumes zero point zero two zero zero mole hydroxide. Its phosphorus oxidation number is plus three by hydrogen plus one and oxygen minus two bookkeeping. The corresponding oxidation numbers in the other two acids are plus one and plus five. Basicity counts the relevant ionizable hydrogens; oxidation number is a different formal quantity. Neither count alone determines the numerical acid dissociation constants or the actual titration endpoint under unspecified conditions.

chapters.title: Ozone resonance does not mean alternating molecules
chapters.formula: O₃: 18 valence electrons; equivalent O–O links in the resonance hybrid
chapters.script: Oxygen has molecular allotropes with different structures. Ozone contains three oxygen atoms and eighteen valence electrons. Its usual octet Lewis contributors each have one single oxygen oxygen bond and one double bond, with the central oxygen carrying formal charge plus one and the singly bonded terminal oxygen minus one. The two contributors exchange electron placement, not atomic positions. They describe one bent molecule with equivalent oxygen oxygen links, rather than a molecule repeatedly switching between two unequal bond arrangements. Averaging the single and double bond labels gives one point five per link in this introductory resonance description. This is an illustrative Lewis bond order, not a complete molecular orbital calculation. Ozone is not simply three separate oxygen atoms, and its structure and reactivity cannot be copied from diatomic oxygen. The molecular formulas also imply different molar masses: using oxygen sixteen, ozone has forty eight grams per mole and dioxygen thirty two. A comparison of equal mole amounts therefore differs from a comparison of equal masses. Keep molecular identity, electron count and counted amount separate.

chapters.title: Carbon allotropes connect structure to properties
chapters.formula: Diamond: 3D four-connected network; graphite: three-connected layers; C₆₀: molecules
chapters.script: Different allotropes contain the same element but organize its atoms differently. In diamond, each carbon has four near neighbours in a three dimensional covalent network. In graphite, each carbon has three near neighbours within extended layers, with delocalized electrons contributing to electrical conduction, especially along those layers. Weak interlayer attractions help explain easy sliding, while the strong bonding inside a layer remains important. These descriptions do not make graphite a collection of isolated six carbon molecules. Buckminsterfullerene instead consists of discrete sixty carbon cage molecules, with each carbon connected to three neighbours in the ideal cage. Counting every cage edge once gives sixty times three divided by two, or ninety carbon carbon connections. Using supplied carbon atomic mass twelve, a mole of these cage molecules has mass seven hundred twenty grams. A mole of carbon atoms still has mass twelve grams regardless of allotrope. Pure ordinary diamond is an electrical insulator, but defects, doping and measurement conditions can alter actual materials. Relate properties to connectivity and electronic structure rather than assigning one universal property to elemental carbon.

chapters.title: Lower oxidation states change oxidizing behaviour
chapters.formula: Selected heavier states: Tl(I), Pb(II), Bi(III); PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2I⁻ → Pb²⁺ + I₂ + 2H₂O
chapters.script: The inert pair trend helps organize the increasing importance of lower oxidation states for some heavier p block elements. Thallium one, lead two and bismuth three are familiar lower states, while higher states can act as oxidants in suitable compounds and media. This is not a rule that every lower state is always the only stable one. Consider lead dioxide reacting with iodide in a supplied acidic model. Lead begins in oxidation state plus four and ends as lead two, accepting two electrons per lead atom. Two iodide ions lose those two electrons to form one iodine molecule. Balancing oxygen and hydrogen gives one lead dioxide, four hydrogen ions and two iodide ions forming one lead two ion, one iodine and two waters. Thus zero point zero one zero zero mole lead dioxide corresponds theoretically to the same amount of iodine and twice that amount of iodide. The compound and medium are essential: an oxidation number alone is not a complete redox potential. Treat this as a balanced evidence example supporting a periodic trend, not an experimental recipe or a claim that every historical p block preparation is required.

chapters.title: Nitrogen dioxide dimerization is not disproportionation
chapters.formula: 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ keeps N at +4; 2NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₂ + HNO₃ gives N(+3) and N(+5)
chapters.script: Different reactions of the same nitrogen oxide can involve different kinds of chemical change. Nitrogen dioxide has nitrogen in oxidation state plus four. When two nitrogen dioxide molecules combine to form dinitrogen tetroxide, each nitrogen remains plus four. That dimerization changes molecular association but is not a redox reaction by oxidation number accounting. In a separate simplified water reaction, two nitrogen dioxide molecules and one water give one nitrous acid and one nitric acid. Nitrogen is plus three in nitrous acid and plus five in nitric acid. One nitrogen is reduced by one unit while the other is oxidized by one, so this net equation represents disproportionation. It preserves two nitrogen atoms, five oxygen atoms and two hydrogens. The acid product mixture is not described by merely assigning both nitrogens the average value plus four and ignoring their individual environments. Real aqueous nitrogen oxide chemistry can involve further reactions and conditions, so this equation is a stated introductory model. Decide whether oxidation states change before classifying a reaction from a familiar formula or from a colour observation alone.

chapters.title: An oxygen bridge is not always a peroxide
chapters.formula: H₂SO₅ and H₂S₂O₈ contain O–O; H₂S₂O₇ has S–O–S; sulfur remains +6
chapters.script: Sulfur oxoacid formulas illustrate why oxidation state assignments need connectivity. In peroxomonosulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur oxygen five, one oxygen oxygen linkage contains two peroxide oxygens. Assign each of those oxygens minus one and the other three minus two. With two hydrogens at plus one, sulfur is plus six, not plus eight. Peroxodisulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur two oxygen eight, also contains one oxygen oxygen linkage. Its two peroxide oxygens contribute minus two together, while six ordinary oxygens contribute minus twelve. The two sulfur atoms therefore contribute plus twelve in total, or plus six each in the usual symmetric structure. Disulfuric acid, hydrogen two sulfur two oxygen seven, instead has an oxygen bridging two sulfur centres and no peroxide linkage. All seven oxygens have their ordinary minus two assignment, again giving sulfur plus six. Counting two sulfur atoms or an oxygen bridge alone does not establish a peroxide. Inspect whether there is an actual oxygen oxygen bond. These are formal structural and charge ledgers, not directions for preparing or handling strongly reactive oxidizing substances.
points: H₂SO₅: one O–O linkage · Two O at −1; three O at −2 · Sulfur +6
H₂S₂O₈: one O–O linkage · Two O at −1; six O at −2 · Each sulfur +6
H₂S₂O₇: S–O–S bridge · No O–O; all seven O at −2 · Each sulfur +6; not a peroxide

Two O at −1; six O at −2
No O–O; all seven O at −2

chapters.title: Xenon oxides and oxyfluorides need full electron counts
chapters.formula: XeOF₄: square pyramidal; XeO₃: trigonal pyramidal; XeO₄: tetrahedral in the introductory model
chapters.script: Noble gas compounds show why a filled shell is not an absolute ban on bonding. Compare three xenon compounds using formal Lewis electron counting and a qualitative electron domain model. Xenon oxyfluoride with one oxygen and four fluorines has forty two valence electrons. A drawing with four single xenon fluorine bonds and one double xenon oxygen bond leaves one central lone pair after terminal octets are completed. Five bonding domains and one lone pair give an octahedral domain arrangement and a square pyramidal molecular shape. Xenon trioxide has twenty six valence electrons. Three formal double xenon oxygen bonds and terminal oxygen lone pairs leave one xenon lone pair, giving three bonding domains and a trigonal pyramidal shape. Xenon tetroxide has thirty two valence electrons and four bonding domains with no central lone pair in the corresponding formal drawing, giving tetrahedral geometry. A multiple bond counts as one domain for this purpose. These models do not require asserting literal d orbital expansion as the bonding mechanism. Oxidation state is plus six in the first two compounds and plus eight in xenon tetroxide.
points: XeOF₄: 42 valence electrons · Five bond domains + one lone pair · Square pyramidal; Xe +6
XeO₃: 26 valence electrons · Three bond domains + one lone pair · Trigonal pyramidal; Xe +6
XeO₄: 32 valence electrons · Four bond domains, no lone pair · Tetrahedral; Xe +8

quiz.question: ns2 np4 is the usual outer configuration of:
quiz.explanation: Two s and four p valence electrons correspond to Group 16 in the p-block pattern.

quiz.question: The noble gas not described by ns2 np6 is:
quiz.explanation: Helium's filled shell is 1s2; it has no occupied valence p subshell.

quiz.question: The first electron-gain enthalpy is more negative for which pair member?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine is less crowded for the added electron, producing this familiar exception to a simple trend.

quiz.question: Water's boiling-point anomaly among these hydrides is explained mainly by:
quiz.explanation: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding raises water's boiling point compared with a simple mass-based trend.

quiz.question: Greater relative stability of Pb(II) down Group 14 is commonly discussed using:
quiz.explanation: The lower +2 state becomes relatively more important for the heavier group member.

quiz.question: Ordinary solid SiO2 is best described here as:
quiz.explanation: Its common solid structures consist of extended Si-O bonding rather than separate CO2-like molecules.

quiz.question: Outer configuration 3s2 3p3 corresponds to:
quiz.explanation: Five main-group outer electrons give group 15; the outer principal shell is 3.

quiz.question: The oxidation number of each oxygen in H2O2 is:
quiz.explanation: Two +1 hydrogens require a total −2 over two oxygens.

quiz.question: The oxygen oxidation number in OF2 is:
quiz.explanation: Two fluorines at −1 require oxygen at +2 for a neutral molecule.

quiz.question: The average oxygen oxidation number in potassium superoxide KO2 is:
quiz.explanation: K contributes +1; the two oxygens together contribute −1, an average −½ each.

quiz.question: BF3 acts as a Lewis acid by:
options: Donating a proton in every reaction
Always losing fluorine as a metal
quiz.explanation: Boron trifluoride can accept an electron pair from a suitable donor.

quiz.question: Xenon compounds show that noble-gas inertness:
options: Requires xenon to have no electrons
Makes every noble gas equally reactive
quiz.explanation: Some heavier noble gases form compounds under suitable conditions.

quiz.question: The number of P–P single bonds in one tetrahedral molecular white P4 unit is:
quiz.explanation: Each of four P atoms connects to three neighbours; divide 4×3 by two because each edge was counted twice.

quiz.question: In the elementary diborane description, four terminal bonds use eight electrons. The two three-centre bridges together use:
quiz.explanation: B2H6 has twelve valence electrons; after eight in terminal bonds, two bridge pairs use the remaining four.

quiz.question: In the idealized net equation SiCl4 + aH2O → SiO2 + 4HCl, a is:
quiz.explanation: Two waters supply two oxygen atoms and four hydrogens. This net endpoint differs from initial Si(OH)4 accounting.

quiz.question: With H=+1 and O=−2, the chlorine oxidation state in HClO4 is:
quiz.explanation: Charge balance gives 1+x−8=0, hence x=+7. Fluorine rules do not determine chlorine in an oxoacid.

quiz.question: The usual controlled comparison for one-oxygen hypohalous acids is:
options: All must have equal intrinsic strength
HF > HOCl is the same comparison
quiz.explanation: Holding the oxygen pattern fixed gives the usual HOCl, HOBr, HOI decreasing strength comparison.

quiz.question: The molecular shape of BrF5 in the elementary six-domain model is:
quiz.explanation: Five bonds and one central lone pair give AX5E: octahedral electron-domain geometry and square pyramidal atomic shape.

quiz.question: In its usual aqueous Lewis-acid description, B(OH)3 accepts an electron pair to form:
options: B3+ as the only dissolved species
quiz.explanation: Hydroxide donates an electron pair to boron, giving the tetrahydroxyborate anion B(OH)4−.

quiz.question: Boric acid is ordinarily described in water as:
options: A base because it contains OH
quiz.explanation: Its usual aqueous acid behaviour involves formation of B(OH)4−; three formula hydrogens do not imply tribasicity.

quiz.question: Ordinary aqueous basicities of H3PO2, H3PO3 and H3PO4 are respectively:
quiz.explanation: Their usual structures contain one, two and three O–H groups; P–H bonds are not counted in this acid-basicity comparison.

quiz.question: Under stipulated complete neutralization, 0.0100 mol H3PO3 requires hydroxide amount:
quiz.explanation: Phosphorous acid is dibasic in the stated model, so each mole consumes two moles hydroxide.

quiz.question: The total valence-electron count of neutral ozone is:
quiz.explanation: Each of the three oxygen atoms supplies six valence electrons, for a total of eighteen.

quiz.question: The two equivalent ozone Lewis contributors describe:
options: Two molecules in a fast chemical equilibrium
One resonance hybrid with unchanged atomic positions
quiz.explanation: Resonance changes electron placement in the drawings; the actual molecule is one bent structure with equivalent links.

quiz.question: An ideal C60 cage has three neighbours per carbon. Counting each C–C connection once gives:
quiz.explanation: The sum of vertex degrees is 60×3; each edge contributes twice, giving 90 distinct connections.

quiz.question: With carbon atomic mass 12, molar mass of C60 molecules is:
quiz.explanation: Each molecule contains sixty carbon atoms, so its molar mass is 60×12=720 g/mol.

quiz.question: In the supplied acidic PbO2/iodide net reaction, lead changes oxidation state from:
quiz.explanation: PbO2 has lead +4, while the product is Pb2+; each lead accepts two electrons.

quiz.question: For 0.0100 mol PbO2 in that complete net conversion, theoretical I2 and consumed I− amounts are:
quiz.explanation: The balanced net equation has PbO2:I2:I− coefficients 1:1:2.

quiz.question: Why is 2NO2⇌N2O4 not redox by oxidation-number accounting?
quiz.explanation: Each nitrogen is +4 in both NO2 and N2O4; association alone does not imply electron-transfer redox.

quiz.question: In 2NO2+H2O→HNO2+HNO3, nitrogen in the two acid products is respectively:
quiz.explanation: HNO2 has N(+3), HNO3 has N(+5), so the net model disproportionates N(+4).

quiz.question: Assign two peroxide oxygens −1 in H2SO5 and all other oxygens −2. Sulfur oxidation state is:
quiz.explanation: Charge balance gives 2+S−2−6=0, so sulfur is +6.

quiz.question: Which formula has the stated S–O–S bridge without an O–O peroxide linkage?
quiz.explanation: Disulfuric acid H2S2O7 has a bridging oxygen; peroxodisulfuric and peroxomonosulfuric acids contain O–O.

quiz.question: In the introductory electron-domain model, XeOF4 has molecular shape:
quiz.explanation: Five bonded atoms and one central lone pair give six domains and a square pyramidal molecular arrangement.

quiz.question: The corresponding shapes of XeO3 and XeO4 are respectively:
quiz.explanation: The formal domain counts are AX3E for XeO3 and AX4 for XeO4; multiple bonds each count as one domain.
